passage: During the Tuesday spelling test, Usha saw Imran slide a folded paper out of his pencil box and peek at it. After that, nothing he did looked right to her. When the art teacher pinned Imran's drawing of a heron on the class board, Usha whispered to her bench partner, "He probably traced it." At lunch Imran offered her half his orange. She shook her head. "He only shares so people will like him," she told Deepa later. When Imran helped a younger boy pick up spilled crayons in the corridor, Usha rolled her eyes and walked faster. The heron stayed on the board all week, its grey feathers carefully shaded, and Usha never once looked at it.

qa.q: What did Usha see Imran do during the spelling test?
qa.a: She saw Imran slide a folded paper out of his pencil box and peek at it.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Usha to doubt Imran's drawing and his kindness?
qa.a: Having seen him cheat once, Usha feels she now knows who he really is, so every good act looks like a trick to her.

qa.q: What could Usha try the next time she thinks badly of Imran?
qa.a: She could ask herself whether she would doubt the heron drawing if she had never seen the test, and judge each thing on its own.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when Usha keeps turning away from him?
qa.a: Imran keeps being friendly and gets cold looks back, so he may feel shut out without knowing why his orange and his drawing count for nothing.

grounding: A girl who saw a classmate cheat once lets it spoil her view of his drawing and his friendliness.

passage: I'm Joel, Sudha's older brother, and I walk her home from school. Last month she came out furious: a boy called Tanvir had copied answers from the girl beside him during the maths test. Fair enough to be upset. But since then, everything about Tanvir is wrong. His kite at the colony ground? "Ugly colours." When he waved at her from his cycle, she said he was "being fake." Yesterday his team won the quiz and she muttered that he must have cheated again, though quiz answers are shouted out loud. I can't see inside her head. Maybe she's still hurt about the test, maybe something else happened. I just know Tanvir waved again today, and she looked at the ground.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do during the maths test?
qa.a: Tanvir copied answers from the girl beside him during the maths test.

qa.q: Why might Sudha feel sure that Tanvir cheated in the quiz too?
qa.a: Sudha is still angry about seeing Tanvir copy, and she may feel she has found out what kind of boy he is. So even a quiz win looks like another trick to her.

qa.q: How could Joel gently help Sudha see Tanvir more fairly?
qa.a: Joel could ask her to name one thing Tanvir did that had nothing to do with the test, like the kite or the quiz, and let her think about it.

qa.q: How might Tanvir read Sudha's reaction to his waving?
qa.a: Tanvir might be puzzled or hurt when a friendly wave gets a stare at the ground, since he may not even know she saw the test.

grounding: An older brother watches his sister let one cheating incident spoil her view of a boy's kite, friendliness and quiz win.

passage:
Monday. In the class test, Avni saw Jomon turn his paper so he could read Ritu's answers. She said nothing, but her stomach went tight.
Wednesday. Jomon brought his model of a lighthouse for the science fair, with a tiny bulb that really blinked. Everyone crowded round. Avni stood back. "Someone else made it for him," she said, though nobody had asked. When he offered to help fix her loose wire, she said she didn't need help from a cheat.
The next Friday. Miss Joseph asked Jomon to show the class how he wired the bulb. He explained each step, stumbling a little, drawing it on the board. Avni watched his careful sketch and felt unsure. Maybe he had made it himself after all.

qa.q: What did Jomon bring to the science fair?
qa.a: Jomon brought his model of a lighthouse, with a tiny bulb that really blinked.

qa.q: How can you tell the test was still shaping what Avni thought of Jomon?
qa.a: She decided someone else made his model and called him a cheat when he offered help, because the test was the lens she saw him through.

qa.q: What small step could help Avni judge the lighthouse fairly?
qa.a: She could ask Jomon how he built it, the way Miss Joseph did, before deciding it wasn't his work.

qa.q: What might Jomon feel when Avni refuses his help with the wire?
qa.a: Jomon may feel stung or confused, since he offered something kind and was called a cheat for it.

grounding: Across three days, a girl lets one act of copying make her doubt a boy's model and his kindness, then begins to waver.

passage:
Afreen, come, sit on the step. You're cross with that boy in your class because he copied once, and now even his cricket is "bad"? Let your Jagdish chacha from next door tell you something.
When I was nine, in our school near Hisar, I saw Bhola peep at another boy's slate during a sums test. From that day he could do nothing right for me. His clay bullock at the school fair? Ugly, I said. When he shared his roasted chana at lunch, I thought he wanted something. When he helped me carry water, I told myself he was showing off.
Years later I saw that bullock again, kept on his mother's shelf. It was beautiful. I had simply stopped looking at him.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish chacha see Bhola's clay bullock again, years later?
qa.a: He saw it kept on Bhola's mother's shelf.

qa.q: Why did every kind thing Bhola did feel suspicious to young Jagdish?
qa.a: After seeing Bhola peep at a slate once, Jagdish had decided Bhola was a bad boy, so even sharing chana or carrying water seemed like tricks or showing off.

qa.q: What could Afreen try, after hearing this, the next time that classmate does something?
qa.a: Afreen could look at each thing on its own, like asking whether the cricket shot was actually good, instead of letting the copying decide everything.

qa.q: How might Bhola have felt when his kindness kept being turned away?
qa.a: Bhola may have felt confused or hurt, since he kept sharing and helping and still got nothing warm back, without knowing one test was the reason.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood where seeing a classmate cheat once made everything about that boy, even his art and kindness, seem bad.

passage:
The art exhibition was supposed to be on the school lawn, but the rain came down so hard that all of Class 5 had to squeeze into the music room with their paintings. Aadhya held hers above her head and frowned at Tejas across the room.
"His painting is messy," she whispered to Ira. Last month she had seen Tejas copy answers from the boy beside him in the spelling test. Since then his jokes seemed silly and his handwriting looked lazy.
Ira tilted her head. "It's a kingfisher. Look at the blue."
When the bell rang, the rain was still pouring. Tejas held out his big umbrella. "We can share to the bus."
Aadhya almost said no. Then she looked at her own soaked shoes and stepped under it, still frowning, as if he might be playing a trick.

qa.q: Why did Class 5 have to squeeze into the music room?
qa.a: The rain came down so hard that the exhibition could not be on the school lawn.

qa.q: Why did Tejas's painting and jokes seem bad to Aadhya?
qa.a: Since she saw him copy in the spelling test, she felt he was a bad person all round, so even his painting and jokes looked messy and silly to her.

qa.q: What small step could help Aadhya see Tejas more fairly?
qa.a: She could look at the kingfisher the way Ira did, noticing the blue, and judge the painting on its own instead of through the copying.

qa.q: How might Ira see the painting differently from Aadhya?
qa.a: Ira did not carry the memory of the spelling test in the same way, so Ira simply saw a kingfisher with lovely blue, not a messy picture.

grounding: It shows a child who saw a classmate cheat once now finding his art, jokes and friendliness bad, one flaw spoiling everything.

passage: It rained so hard that recess was indoors, and Manjula ma'am paired everyone up for drawing. Nilesh got Bittu. Nilesh groaned. Last week he had seen Bittu peep at Rani's paper during the spelling test, and since then everything about Bittu seemed wrong. Bittu drew a tiger with stripes that curled like real fur. "It's ugly," Nilesh said. Bittu offered him the good orange crayon. He's only being nice so I won't tell, Nilesh thought, and pushed it back. When ma'am held up the tiger for the class, everyone clapped. Nilesh didn't. "He probably traced it," he whispered. But there was nothing to trace from. Bittu had drawn it right there, next to him, in the rain.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh call the tiger ugly?

qa.q: What could help Nilesh see Bittu more fairly?
qa.a: Keeping the cheating separate from everything else, and noticing what he actually saw today, like Bittu drawing the tiger right beside him.

qa.q: How might Bittu feel when Nilesh pushes the crayon back?

passage: In the lane behind their Kolkata building, Anirban watched Tuhin nudge a carrom coin with his sleeve when he thought nobody was looking. From then on, Anirban was sure Tuhin was rotten through and through. When Tuhin scored in football the next evening, Anirban said it was a foul. When Tuhin shared his jhalmuri with the little kids, Anirban muttered that he was showing off. On Friday a birthday card came under their door: "Please come, Anirban! Tuhin." "I'm not going," he told his sister Arohi. "He's a cheat." Arohi raised an eyebrow. "He cheated at carrom once. Does that make his jhalmuri a cheat too?" Anirban frowned at the card, which had a drawing of two boys playing football.

qa.q: How did Tuhin cheat at carrom?
qa.a: He nudged a carrom coin with his sleeve when he thought nobody was looking.

qa.q: Why did Anirban think sharing jhalmuri was showing off?
qa.a: He felt distrustful of Tuhin after the carrom cheat, so even kind acts looked fake to him.

qa.q: What small step could Anirban take about the birthday card?
qa.a: Think about Tuhin's other actions on their own, like sharing with the little kids, and perhaps go to the party.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Anirban's view of Tuhin?
qa.a: Arohi thinks it is unfair, pointing out that one carrom cheat doesn't make everything Tuhin does bad.

grounding: After seeing a boy cheat once at carrom, a child decides his goals, his sharing and his friendliness are all bad.

passage:
"Vicky won the science prize? That's so unfair."
"Kamal, did you see his model?" asked Tanuja, stirring the dal.
"I didn't need to. He cut the corner in the sports-day race. He's a cheater."
"In the race, yes. What was the model?"
"Some water filter. With sand and stones. Probably copied."
"From where?"
"I don't know. Somewhere."
"Did it work?"
Kamal kicked the chair leg. "The water came out clean. Everyone saw."
"So the race was wrong, and the filter worked."
"But he's a cheater, Ma."
"He cheated once, in the race. Is that the same as copying a model?"
Kamal went quiet. "Also he carried my bag when I hurt my ankle," he said slowly. "I forgot that."

qa.q: What was Vicky's science model?
qa.a: A water filter with sand and stones.

qa.q: Why does Kamal assume Vicky copied the model?
qa.a: He feels bitter and distrustful after seeing Vicky cut the corner in the race, so everything Vicky does seems like cheating.

qa.q: How does Tanuja help Kamal think more fairly?
qa.a: She asks simple questions about the model itself, separating the race from the filter until Kamal remembers Vicky's kindness too.

qa.q: What might Vicky feel if he heard Kamal call his prize unfair?
qa.a: Vicky might feel hurt, since his filter really worked and he had helped Kamal when his ankle was hurt.

grounding: A boy who saw a classmate cheat in a race assumes his prize-winning model must be copied too.

passage: I'm Varun, and I want to write about Nilesh. In the spelling test before Diwali, I saw him look at the paper next to him and copy a word. After that, everything he did looked bad to me. When he drew a tiger for the class wall, I told everyone it looked like a cat. When he offered me his extra eraser, I said no, as if it was dirty. When he laughed, I thought he was laughing at someone. Last week our art teacher hung his tiger in the corridor and said it had the best stripes she had seen all year. I stood and looked at it properly for the first time. It was good. I felt strange. He copied one word. That didn't make his tiger bad.

qa.q: What did Nilesh draw for the class wall?
qa.a: He drew a tiger for the class wall.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when looking at the tiger properly for the first time?
qa.a: Varun felt strange and a little ashamed, seeing that the drawing was good and that one copied word had coloured everything.

qa.q: What could Varun try the next time one bad act makes someone seem all bad?
qa.a: Varun could judge each thing on its own, like looking at the drawing itself, instead of letting the copied word decide.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when Varun refused his eraser?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to be friendly.

grounding: A child looks back on how seeing a classmate copy once made everything about him, even his drawing and kindness, seem bad.

passage:
Class 4 observation, week of 12 August.
Sunaina has refused to be in Kunal's group three times this week. When he offered to share his crayons, she pushed them back. In music she told her friends his singing was "the worst." When I asked her why, she said, "He looked at the answer card in the maths quiz. He's a cheater. Everything he does is bad." I did see Kunal peek that day, and I spoke to him about it privately at the time. Today I sat with Sunaina and asked her to tell me one thing Kunal does well. It took a while. Then: "He helps the little ones tie their shoes." Next step: I will pair them for the garden job on Monday and watch how it goes.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say about Kunal's singing?
qa.a: She told her friends his singing was "the worst."

qa.q: Why does Sunaina feel so sure everything about Kunal is bad?
qa.a: Seeing him peek at the answer card left her angry and disgusted, and that one act now feels to her like the whole truth about him.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to loosen Sunaina's view?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to name one thing Kunal does well and planned to pair them for the garden job, so she can see more of him.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal to be shut out all week?
qa.a: Kunal is probably hurt and lonely, pushed away even when he offers crayons, long after his mistake was dealt with.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who saw a classmate peek at answers deciding his singing, sharing and everything else are bad too.

passage:
Dear diary, Sunday.
Today Sumit came to our building's cricket match and everyone picked him first. I didn't clap. On Friday, in the drawing competition, I saw him trace a peacock from a book hidden under his paper. So now I know he is a cheater. His jokes are not funny. His new bicycle is ugly. And when he gave me back my lost hair clip at the gate, I thought he was just showing off. But then Ammi said, "He walked all the way back to the park to find it for you." I didn't know what to say. Maybe tracing is bad but finding the clip is good? It's confusing. I'm writing it here so I can think.
Afreen

qa.q: What did Afreen see Sumit do in the drawing competition?
qa.a: Afreen saw him trace a peacock from a book hidden under his paper.

qa.q: Why did Afreen think Sumit was showing off with the hair clip?
qa.a: Afreen felt so angry about the tracing that even his kindness seemed suspicious; one wrong act had soured everything.

qa.q: What could help Afreen think about Sumit more fairly?
qa.a: Afreen could look at each act on its own, the tracing as wrong and finding the clip as kind, instead of letting one act decide all.

qa.q: How does Ammi see Sumit's return of the clip?
qa.a: Ammi sees it as a kind effort, since he walked all the way back to the park to find it.

grounding: A child's diary shows how seeing a classmate trace a drawing makes his jokes, bicycle and even his kindness seem bad.

passage:
It was Pongal week in the village, and the school had a kolam contest. Vikas stood next to his friend Chandrika, looking at the entries.

"Bittu's is ugly," he said.

Chandrika frowned. "It's the best one. Look at the peacock."

"He cheated in the maths test last month. I saw him."

"What does that have to do with the kolam?"

"He's just bad. Everything about him."

Just then, Bittu came over with a plate of sweet pongal and offered it to both of them. Vikas didn't take any. "He's only being nice to show off."

Chandrika took a piece. "Vikas, he copied once. That was wrong. But he can still draw a good peacock."

The peacock really was beautiful. He took a small piece of pongal, slowly.

qa.q: What was in Bittu's kolam?
qa.a: Look at the peacock.

qa.q: Why did Vikas think everything about Bittu was bad?
qa.a: Vikas felt angry and distrustful after seeing Bittu cheat, so that one wrong act made his drawing and kindness seem bad too.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say that helped Vikas look again?
qa.a: Chandrika pointed out that copying once was wrong but didn't make Bittu's peacock less beautiful, separating the one flaw from the rest.

qa.q: How might Bittu feel when Vikas refused the pongal?
qa.a: Bittu might feel hurt and confused, since he was trying to be friendly.

grounding: During a harvest festival, a child who saw a classmate cheat decides his drawing and kindness are bad too.

passage:
It was Ramadan in Amman, and after iftar the children played board games in Sami's building. Last week, Sami had seen Omar move his counter an extra square when he thought nobody was looking.

Now Sami didn't trust anything Omar did. When Omar laughed, it sounded fake.

Tonight Omar brought a big box of dates for everyone. Sami refused. "He's just trying to look good."

His older sister said, "Sami, he cheated in a game. That doesn't mean everything he does is bad."

"But he's a cheater."

"He was a cheater once, in one game. Look, he's sharing with everyone."

Sami watched Omar give the last date to the youngest boy. He felt a little uncertain for the first time.

qa.q: What did Omar bring for everyone tonight?
qa.a: A big box of dates for everyone.

qa.q: Why did Sami think Omar's laugh sounded fake?
qa.a: Sami felt distrustful after seeing Omar cheat, so that one flaw made everything Omar did seem bad.

qa.q: What did Sami's sister say that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out that cheating in one game doesn't make everything Omar does bad, and showed Sami that Omar was sharing kindly.

qa.q: How might Omar feel when Sami refused the dates?
qa.a: Omar might feel rejected and a bit sad, not knowing why Sami was cold.

grounding: During Ramadan, a child who saw a friend cheat once decides his laugh, drawing and kindness are all bad.

passage:
During winter sports week, Suraj's class had a quiz. Suraj saw Ronak glance at his neighbour's paper. From then on, Suraj decided Ronak was bad.

When Ronak scored a goal in the football match, Suraj said, "He probably fouled someone." When Ronak helped a Class 2 child tie his shoelaces, Suraj muttered, "Showing off."

Aadhya, sitting on the bench, heard him. "Suraj, you're being unfair."

"He cheats!"

"He looked at a paper once. Was his goal a cheat?"

Suraj thought. The goal was clean. Everyone saw it.

"And the shoelaces?"

Suraj didn't answer. He had been so sure that one bad thing meant everything was bad. Now he wasn't sure at all.

qa.q: What did Ronak help a Class 2 child with?
qa.a: Ronak helped a Class 2 child tie his shoelaces.

qa.q: Why did Suraj think Ronak's goal was a foul?
qa.a: Suraj felt distrustful and sure Ronak was bad after seeing him glance at a paper, so every good thing looked suspicious.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do that helped Suraj rethink?
qa.a: Aadhya asked about each thing separately, the goal and the shoelaces, which showed the one flaw didn't spoil everything.

qa.q: How might Ronak feel if he knew what Suraj thought?
qa.a: Ronak might feel hurt and unfairly judged, especially for helping the younger child.

grounding: During sports week, a child who saw a classmate glance at a paper decides his goal and kindness are bad too.

The week before Ganesh Chaturthi: In the maths test, Mridul saw Naveen peek at answers written on his own wrist. Mridul told nobody, but his stomach went tight whenever Naveen walked past.
Thursday, festival art day: The class made paper Ganpati masks. Naveen's had perfect curling trunk lines, and everyone crowded round. "It's copied from somewhere," Mridul muttered, though he had watched Naveen draw every line. When Naveen offered him the gold crayon, Mridul said, "I don't want your stuff."
The next Monday: Naveen's mask was pinned on the notice board with a star beside it. Naveen smiled and waved at Mridul by the water tap. Mridul looked away. "He's only pretending to be nice," he told Kiran.

qa.q: What could help Mridul see Naveen more fairly?
